entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
20th Century Studios (formerly 20th Century Fox) is one of Hollywood's oldest major studios, founded in 1935 through the merger of Fox Film Corporation and Twentieth Century Pictures. For nearly 90 years, the studio has been responsible for some of cinema's most commercially successful and culturally significant films: The Sound of Music (1965), Star Wars (1977), Alien (1979), Die Hard (1988), Home Alone (1990), Titanic (1997), and Avatar (2009-2022).

Darryl F. Zanuck, who ran Fox from 1935-1971, built the studio into a powerhouse through an unusual commitment to serious dramatic films alongside blockbusters — The Grapes of Wrath (1940), How Green Was My Valley (1941), Gentleman's Agreement (1947), and All About Eve (1950) were all 20th Century Fox productions. The studio's 20th Century Fox lot in Century City, Los Angeles, was once the largest in Hollywood.

Rupert Murdoch's News Corporation acquired Fox in 1985, transforming it into part of a global media empire. George Lucas's Star Wars changed the studio's fortunes — Lucas negotiated unprecedented sequel and merchandising rights, laying the foundation for franchise filmmaking. James Cameron's Titanic (1997, $1.84 billion) and Avatar (2009, $2.9 billion, then the highest-grossing film ever) were Fox productions. Disney acquired the studio in 2019 for $71 billion, renaming it 20th Century Studios and removing the 'Fox' branding.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: 20th Century Fox's production of Star Wars (1977) revolutionized franchise filmmaking, while Avatar and Titanic set all-time box office records — and its $71 billion Disney acquisition restructured Hollywood's entire studio landscape.
